principalConclusion: ARA must separate learner autonomy, self-regulation support, adaptation, accessibility and AI assistance into distinct but composable dimensions. Autonomy is not unlimited choice; adaptation is not accommodation; accessibility is a rights- and barrier-oriented overlay rather than an optional personalization feature; and AI remains a bounded assistant whose proposals, drafts and recommendations require visible status, inspectability, editability, contestability, validation and role-appropriate human authority.
recommendedPath: Preserve the AraLearn reference profile: explicit user control, authored structure, minimal functional state, live-AI independence for study, and MCP-assisted authoring/audit/repair with explicit application.

Adopt shared control: authors and protocols define coherent constraints; learners control pace and permitted choices; accessibility and participant rights have higher precedence; automated rules and AI remain subordinate.
Represent self-regulation through optional, explicit supports for goals, planning, monitoring, strategies, help seeking, reflection and self-evaluation rather than inferring a learner trait.
Accept adaptation only when target, trigger, evidence basis, authority, application mode, transparency, override, rollback, snapshot and fallback are explicit.
Use recommendation-and-confirm or preview-only as the default for AI- or model-proposed adaptations; defer silent automatic application.

Treat accessibility as a baseline design obligation plus protected accommodations, with WCAG 2.2, UDL-informed options, assistive-technology testing, equivalence review, construct preservation and minimal disclosure.
Separate AI functions for planning, microsequence composition, card generation, explanation, hints, critique, audit, repair, translation, comparison and configuration recommendation.

Use two complementary user channels: chat/MCP for natural-language direction and ARA for real-time rendering, deterministic operations, version selection, comments, diffs, approval and repair requests.
Keep every AI output in an explicit lifecycle from suggestion/draft to validation, audit, human approval and publication; AI cannot promote its own output.
Require bounded context, grounding, provenance, model/provider policy, user editability, contestation, deterministic validation where possible and explicit failure/offline behavior.
Preserve cognitive effort in AI-assisted study through optional prediction, explanation, critique or reflection steps; do not use AI as universal answer substitution.
Use named profiles and sparse overrides so GPT and nontechnical users do not have to declare the full parameter catalogue in every course artifact.

Defer product, storage and architecture decisions for microsequence-first composition, manifests, IndexedDB materialization and synchronization to Issues #6 and #7 while preserving them as concrete required inputs.

deferredCandidates.reason: Requires valid constructs, authorized observables, calibration, transparency, contestability, governance and cross-context evaluation.
Attempts, time, delay, interruption, help use and comments are not direct measures of struggle.
Expertise is domain- and task-specific and cannot be inferred safely from structural progress or interaction traces alone.
Would combine content transformation, sequencing, accessibility, authority and publication without an accepted domain or architecture.
Raises content validity, provenance, offline, cost, accessibility, consistency and experimental-comparability problems.
Validity, fairness, contestability and consequential authority remain insufficient.

deferredCandidates.destination: rejected unless future compelling ethical/legal evidence
deferredCandidates.reason: Highly sensitive constructs, weak proxies and unacceptable privacy/discrimination risk.
Accommodations require learner involvement, construct review and privacy; model output cannot be treated as entitlement decision.
Consent, licensing, confidentiality, retention, deletion and model-governance questions are unresolved.
Requires accepted microsequence/reference model, permissions, provenance, versioning and impact analysis.

rejectedOrNotRecommended: Unlimited learner control as a universal default.
Treating absence of self-regulation prompts or user planning as learner deficit.
Inferring motivation, effort, expertise, disability, struggle or engagement from raw interaction signals.
Hidden adaptation or adaptation applied without visible target, reason and effective-state record.
Accessibility as an optional profile that can be disabled instead of a baseline and precedence rule.
Requiring public or author-visible disability disclosure to obtain ordinary accessible options.
Assuming every alternative modality is educationally equivalent without construct review.
AI as teacher, final editor, publisher or consequential evaluator by default.
Treating AI-generated text as verified because it is fluent, cited or reviewed by another AI.
Using explanations or confidence scores alone as safeguards against automation bias.
All-or-nothing acceptance of AI output or silent mutation of published artifacts.
Unbounded MCP context, cross-workspace retrieval or retention of full conversations by default.
Silent provider/model substitution, silent online-only behavior or silent fallback to lower-quality AI.
Mandatory AI assistance in the baseline study path.
Automatic answer provision that replaces the cognitive operation the learner is intended to practice.
Collecting AI interaction events merely because the system can emit them.
risks: Parameter explosion and confusing precedence across learner, author, protocol, institution, accessibility and AI.
Autonomy rhetoric masking abandonment, overload or manipulative choice architecture.
Adaptive recommendations built on invalid proxies and presented as objective.
Overreliance, automation bias and deskilling when AI drafts or recommendations are easy to accept.
Algorithm aversion and abandonment if users cannot inspect or modify imperfect suggestions.
Accessibility options changing the construct without transparent qualification.
Forced disclosure or leakage of disability and accommodation information.
AI assistance reproducing bias, hallucinated dependencies, fabricated sources or homogenized course design.
Human review becoming ceremonial rather than substantive.
Independent AI audit being mistaken for independent evidence.
Connected AI breaking offline continuity or creating provider lock-in.
Research conditions becoming irreproducible when model, context, prompt, configuration or output versions are not preserved.
Nontechnical interfaces hiding consequences so thoroughly that users cannot make informed choices.
Excessive warnings and cognitive forcing creating burden, accessibility problems and avoidance.
Comments and chat context exposing confidential, personal or participant information.
decisionChangingUncertainties: Which autonomy and SRL supports benefit adult worker-students in fragmented, mobile and offline study.
How much learner control is productive by domain, expertise, stakes and course structure.
Which shared-control patterns preserve agency without weakening prerequisites or experimental validity.
What evidence can validly trigger adaptation in ARA without surveillance.
How users understand profiles, sparse overrides, AI status, provenance and consequences.
How cognitive forcing, disclaimers and previews affect overreliance, burden and accessibility in authoring and study.
Validity and transfer of AI tutoring effects beyond narrow domains, institutions and short interventions.
Whether AI-assisted study preserves unaided performance and long-term transfer.
How to evaluate AI-generated course variants for content equivalence and accidental confounds.
How accessibility accommodations should be represented and snapshotted without exposing sensitive information.
Which AI functions must remain connected, can be local, or require deterministic alternatives.
How provider/model changes affect research equivalence and published-course maintenance.
How microsequence-first composition changes authoring authority, reuse, repair and user comprehension.
How nontechnical teachers, tutors, researchers and self-directed learners manage advanced configuration without losing control.
Transfer to Brazilian, Portuguese and other non-WEIRD educational and institutional contexts.
